description:
Wesam Saad begins defending the timing of the rapture after reviewing the resurrection and reward outline. He answers why Old Testament saints receive their bodily resurrection later in his model, while affirming one salvation through faith in the Messiah. He also rejects a partial rapture of only some born-again Christians. His expectation of Christ's coming does not depend on identifying a world government, economic event or the last person to be saved. Before presenting contrasts, he states the assumptions carried forward from earlier sessions: premillennialism and a distinction between Israel and the church.

The main case tests a posttribulation rapture within that framework. Saad asks how an immediate return to earth fits the dwelling places in the Father's house, who populates the millennial kingdom if every believer is already glorified, and how the rescue at the Mount of Olives fits that sequence. He also considers the sheep-and-goats judgment and believers' rewards. These are his proposed difficulties for a competing position, rather than a record of complete replies from its advocates. Questions clarify that Jewish Christians belong to the church and that the rapture is not restricted to Gentiles. His purpose is to build the case in stages, with further teaching about Daniel and the tribulation still ahead.

questions.question: Does Saad teach a different means of salvation for earlier saints?
questions.answer: No. He explicitly says salvation is through faith in the Messiah for both groups, while assigning their resurrection and rewards to different points in his model. The distinction concerns the ages and assessment, not an alternative way of being saved by law.

questions.question: Who is included in the rapture as he describes it?
questions.answer: Saad affirms all born-again Christians, using the promise that all will be changed. He later rejects restricting the event to Gentile believers, noting that Paul himself is Jewish and speaks of we all. Profession without new birth is not the category he is affirming.

questions.question: What observable conditions does he require before expecting the rapture?
questions.answer: He says believers need not wait for an identifiable economic arrangement, world government or other public sign. God knows his own appointed plan, but people cannot identify the final person to be saved and use that knowledge as a clock. His emphasis is eager expectation rather than date setting.

questions.question: Which assumptions does he carry into the argument?
questions.answer: Saad states premillennialism and a distinction between Israel and the church as positions already defended in the course. The present argument builds on them rather than proving them again. Its conclusions should be read with those stated assumptions in view.

questions.question: How does he classify Jewish people who are Christians in the present age?
questions.answer: He expressly affirms that they are in Christ and part of the church. In his model that does not cancel future promises he associates with Jewish identity. He leaves the determination of that identity to God, rather than providing a human genetic test or a criterion of personal worth.

questions.question: How does he use the Father's house in John 14?
questions.answer: Saad understands Christ's promise to prepare a place and receive his people as involving time with him in the Father's house. He asks how that fits a rapture followed immediately by a return to earth. This is his interpretation of the promise within the framework he has stated.

questions.question: How does the class qualify the scope of that comparison?
questions.answer: A participant notes that the argument has a particular force within a premillennial model. Saad reaffirms that premillennialism is his stated assumption. He also acknowledges that his more extensive conversations have been with other positions, rather than presenting complete posttribulation replies in this recording.

questions.question: What question does he raise about populating the millennial kingdom?
questions.answer: Saad asks who remains in ordinary bodies to have children if all believers are glorified at Christ's return and unbelievers are judged. He sees the need for mortal believers entering the kingdom as a difficulty for the posttribulation sequence he is testing.

questions.question: How does the Mount of Olives rescue enter his argument?
questions.answer: He connects Zechariah's physical escape route with believers still needing rescue on earth. He asks where their rapture fits if all believers should already have been glorified in the clouds. This remains his sequence argument from the passages, not an independently proved answer to every opposing reading.

questions.question: What further difficulty does he raise from the sheep-and-goats judgment?
questions.answer: Saad reads Matthew 25 as separating people for entry into the kingdom and asks how its scene fits people already glorified and rewarded. He uses the question to add weight to his case. Some proposed details about their limited instruction are his explanatory inference rather than an explicit statement in Matthew.
